from research_site import Study

study = Study()
ROMANS = "Test on Romans"
MATTHEW = "Test on Matthew 11–16"

## Summary

- We fine-tuned NLLB on text transcribed by ten speech-recognition (ASR) models, plus one combined transcript, and measured how the transcript's character error rate (CER) relates to BLEU and chrF3.
- The combined transcript has the lowest CER and the highest scores on both test sets.
- On Matthew 11–16, a lower CER goes with higher scores. On Romans, CER is a weak predictor of the scores, and the alignment score with the source text tracks them more closely.
- Each transcript is a single training run, so the study shows a pattern across eleven transcripts, not precise effects.

## The question

Speech recognition lets a team draft text from audio, but its transcripts contain errors. This study asks how the amount of noise in an ASR transcript, measured by CER, affects the translation scores of a model fine-tuned on it.

## How it was tested

Ten ASR models were fine-tuned on the audio of chapters 1–10 of one gospel and used to transcribe the audio of a whole New Testament. A combined transcript was made from the ten transcripts with an LLM. <!-- REVIEW: "with an LLM" is inferred from the transcript's name in the experiment folder; confirm how it was combined. -->

NLLB was fine-tuned with silnlp for each of the eleven transcripts, with the transcript as the target text and a Bible in another language as the source. There is one training run per transcript, with the same random seed.

Four measures are reported for each transcript:

- **chrF3** and **BLEU**: scores of the fine-tuned model's drafts on the test set, from sacrebleu.
- **CER (%)**: the overall character error rate of the ASR model that produced the transcript, on held-out audio. <!-- REVIEW: CER is taken from the researcher's spreadsheet, which lists 35 samples per model; confirm what it was measured against. -->
- **Alignment score**: how regularly the transcript's words align with the source text, from word alignment with eflomal. Higher is better. <!-- REVIEW: the sheet's alignment scores for the Matthew 11–16 tab come from fast_align (0.27–0.31); this study uses the eflomal scores from the Romans tab for both tables, since the training text is the same. Confirm. -->

### What the results show

- **The combined transcript is best.** It has the lowest CER (5.48%) and the highest chrF3 on both tests (66.5 on Matthew 11–16, 48.7 on Romans). On Romans this is partly expected, because the Romans test text is the combined transcript itself.
- **On Matthew 11–16, less noise means better scores.** chrF3 ranges from 61.0 to 66.5 across the transcripts, and the rank correlation between CER and chrF3 is −0.74 (−0.67 for BLEU). <!-- REVIEW: rank (Spearman) correlations over the 11 transcripts, computed from the tables by the author of this page; not in metrics.csv. -->
- **On Romans, CER predicts little.** chrF3 ranges from 32.2 to 48.7 and BLEU from 3.4 to 11.9, and the rank correlation with CER is only −0.26 (−0.14 for BLEU). For example, ASR models 2 and 4 have similar CERs (6.63% and 6.81%), but chrF3 of 33.6 and 47.1. <!-- REVIEW: same computation as above. -->
- **Alignment with the source tracks the Romans scores better.** The rank correlation between alignment score and chrF3 is 0.82 on Romans (0.63 on Matthew 11–16). This suggests that a transcript's CER alone does not capture what matters for translation. <!-- REVIEW: same computation as above. -->

## Limitations

- **One run per transcript and no intervals.** Differences of a point or two are within noise.
- **Eleven transcripts, one language, one model.** The correlations come from eleven points.
- **CER is measured on a small set of held-out samples**, so it is itself uncertain.
- **The test text is not an independent human reference** in these experiments, so the scores measure agreement with a transcript, not necessarily with correct text.
